the-next.name: The NEXT
aka: The NEXT: Museum, Library, and Preservation Space
the-next.operator: the Electronic Literature Organization (ELO), managed by the Electronic Literature Lab at Washington State University Vancouver; Dene Grigar, Managing Director and Curator; the ELO Repository names the university library as a partner
the-next.kind: a combination museum, library, and preservation space for collections of digital art and writing, in its own words; Wikipedia (third party) calls it a repository of electronic literature
the-next.record_object: born-digital art and writing: author collections donated by artists and scholars, the contents of online experimental journals from 1995 to the present, the Electronic Literature Collections, showcases, scholarly publications, the ELO's own historical media, exhibitions and physical archives

record.in_layer: not recorded: the saved sources say nothing of crawling or training; the home page lists 'Artificial Intelligence (AI)', 'Algorithmic', 'Generative' and 'Combinatory' among the qualities found in its 48 collections, without naming which works carry them
record.name: held by named collection: author collections under the artist's or scholar's name, journals under founder and editors, the ELC volumes under their editors (repository page); Wikipedia (third party) states that the Marjorie C. Luesebrink Collection keeps 27 works published under the pen name M.D. Coverley; work-level metadata fields are not shown in the saved sources, and no attribution rule for generated text is stated
record.readback: browse by category and a Basic Search on the home page; per Wikipedia (third party), works on obsolete software are re-created by migration to newer systems, the Pathfinders project recorded 'traversals' (video and audio of works on historically appropriate platforms), and an Extended Electronic Metadata Schema (ELMS) describes each work and its reading issues; where re-creation is not yet possible, only metadata is provided
record.makes: no machine composition is recorded; what the preservation apparatus makes from a work is recorded (Wikipedia, third party): re-created and re-imagined versions on newer systems, video playthroughs, traversal recordings, and metadata standing in for works that cannot yet be run

lifecycle.detail: the home page announces a new work (ThinkingDaughters) and an expanded exhibition; the saved repository page still marks several collections as coming soon

the-next.founded: 2011 per Wikipedia (third party), whose text dates the opening to 'the lab'; the saved own pages give no founding date
the-next.tll_reading: The archive reads The NEXT as the preservation house of the procedural lineage #186 names, where the machine is method, and as the field's working practice of readback: a work held there is kept under its author's or journal's name and read back by migration, re-creation, recorded traversal or metadata, which is a reception history carried out by an institutional apparatus. Its own pages list 'Artificial Intelligence (AI)' and 'Generative' among its qualities and say nothing of a machine reader or of training, so whether any held work belongs to the fourth column of #186, or records machine composition in the sense of #1543, waits on work-level traversal.

self_description.q: Envisioned as a combination museum, library, and preservation space, The NEXT maintains and makes its archives accessible for the next generation and responds to the growing need for open-access, travel-free cultural and research experiences for today's public and scholars.

wp_repository.q: The NEXT: Museum, Library, and Preservation Space is a repository of electronic literature . It is supported by Washington State University at Vancouver and the Electronic Literature Organization .

wp_elms.q: The NEXT uses an Extended Electronic Metadata Schema (ELMS) to describe the complex and interactive digital works it holds. This metadata describes the work and alerts readers to potential reading issues such as fleeting text, color use, or requirements for moving a mouse or moving with a virtual reality environment.

wp_migration.q: The NEXT has re-created these works by migrating them to newer systems.

wp_metadata_limit.q: Where recreating the work is not yet possible, such as Shockwave works like Jim Andrew's Nio , and Noah Wardrip Fruin et al.'s The Impermanence Agent , the NEXT has provided as much metadata as possible.

wp_pen_name.q: Luesebrink created and published 27 of these works under the pen name M.D. Coverley—and the NEXT Museum re-imagined, migrated, and developed video playthroughs of these works as they were written on now-obsolete software.

output-anthology.name: Output: An Anthology of Computer-Generated Text, 1953–2023
output-anthology.operator: edited by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram and Nick Montfort; published by Counterpath, co-published with MIT Press (the Counterpath page is the saved source; its title line prints the first editor's name as 'Lillian Yvonne-Bertram')
output-anthology.kind: in the publisher's words, 'An anthology of seven decades of English-language outputs from computer generation systems'
output-anthology.record_object: English-language texts produced by generation systems and software over seven decades, 1953 to 2023: many types of creative writing, text from research systems, and reports and utilitarian texts

record.in_layer: not recorded: the saved page describes outputs and systems and says nothing of what the systems read or were trained on
record.name: not recorded beyond the editors on the saved page; each excerpt is 'introduced individually', and the page states no rule for how systems, programmers or co-authors are credited
record.readback: 'Bibliographic references allow readers to learn more about outputs and systems that intrigue them', which ties each output back to its system and publication
record.makes: the anthology's object is what generation systems made: outputs across conversations, humor, letters, poetry, prose and sentences, from implemented systems only

lifecycle.detail: a single published volume, October 2024; the page offers copies for purchase and announces no later edition

output-anthology.tll_reading: The archive reads Output as the edited field history of the TM→ direction of #1543, seven decades of what implemented generation systems emitted, with each output traceable to its system by bibliographic reference, and as the procedural lineage #186 names in Montfort's Using Electricity series and Bertram's Travesty Generator. Its object is generated output; the saved page records neither the systems' reading nor any address to a machine reader.

self_description.q: An anthology of seven decades of English-language outputs from computer generation systems, chronicling the vast history of machine-written texts created long before ChatGPT.

silicon_valley.q: text generation, as it happens, was not invented yesterday in Silicon Valley

aim.q: This anthology, Output , thoughtfully selected, introduced, and edited by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram and Nick Montfort, aims to correct that omission by gathering seven decades of English-language texts produced by generation systems and software.

span.q: The outputs span many different types of creative writing and include text generated by research systems, along with reports and utilitarian texts, representing many general advances and experiments in text generation.

encountered.q: Output is first and foremost a collection of outputs to be encountered by readers.

organized.q: In addition to an overall introduction, each of the excerpts is introduced individually and organized by fine-grain genre including conversations, humor, letters, poetry, prose, and sentences.

bibliographic.q: Bibliographic references allow readers to learn more about outputs and systems that intrigue them.

reference_book.q: Although Output could serve as a reference book, it is designed to be readable and to be read.

excluded.q: Purposefully excluded are human–computer collaborations that were conceptually defined but not implemented as a computer system.

title_line.q: Output: An Anthology of Computer-Generated Text, 1953–2023 , edited by Lillian Yvonne-Bertram and Nick Montfort

publication.q: October 2024 co-published with MIT Press edited by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram and Nick Montfort $40.00; 7″ x 9″ 500 pgs. ISBN 978-0262549813.

bertram.q: Lillian-Yvonne Bertram is the author of Travesty Generator , a book of computational poetry that was longlisted for the 2020 National Book Award for Poetry

montfort_series.q: He is the series editor of Counterpath’s Using Electricity series

montfort_post.q: He is Professor of Digital Media at MIT and Principal Investigator in the Center for Digital Narrative at the University of Bergen, Norway.

olmotrace.name: OLMoTrace
aka: OLMoTrace: Tracing Language Model Outputs Back to Trillions of Training Tokens
olmotrace.operator: Ai2 (The Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence), as a feature in the Ai2 Playground; the paper's authors are Jiacheng Liu and 30 others
olmotrace.kind: a feature in the Ai2 Playground that traces language model outputs back to their full training data in real time; its paper calls it a system, released as open source
olmotrace.record_object: verbatim matches between segments of a language model's output and documents in its training corpora, for Ai2's OLMo models (OLMo 2 32B Instruct, OLMo 2 13B Instruct, OLMoE 1B 7B Instruct) and for any model whose training data is accessible

record.in_layer: it matches output against the model's full training data: for OLMo 2 32B Instruct, five datasets across pretraining, mid-training, supervised finetuning, preference learning and RL, about 3.2 billion documents and 4.6 trillion tokens
record.name: not recorded; the side panel shows document snippets from the training data, and the saved sources do not say whether a document's author, title or source address is shown; Ai2 leaves it to the user to 'personally verify that these documents come from trusted sources'
record.readback: yes, for verbatim spans: 'Show OLMoTrace' highlights long and unique spans of a response that appear verbatim in the training data and lists the documents that contain them (up to 10 snippets per span, a random 10 where there are more), ranked by BM25 against the prompt and response; a span may be covered only by parts found in different documents
record.makes: the model's response, of which only long, unique, self-contained spans with a verbatim match are highlighted (K = 0.05 times the response's token count); Ai2 shows it tracing 'creative' expressions, arithmetic and a false knowledge-cutoff claim to training documents, in its own hedged terms ('may have learned', 'could have easily learned it through memorization')

lifecycle.detail: introduced 9 April 2025 as available in the Ai2 Playground; paper v1 9 April 2025, v2 8 July 2025; its availability after that date is unread

olmotrace.tll_reading: An inspection instrument for #1543's FROM direction at the string level: a highlighted span is a witness that a stretch of output has a verbatim antecedent in the training data, the evidence for #1543's source status S = retrieved. Verbatim matching is not causal influence, and productive transformation (W, the generative uptake #1543 scores) leaves no verbatim span to highlight; whether a matched work is carried under its author's name is unrecorded.

self_description.q: Today we introduce OLMoTrace, a one-of-a-kind feature in the Ai2 Playground that lets you trace the outputs of language models back to their full, multi-trillion-token training data in real time.

operator.q: © The Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence - All Rights Reserved.

purpose.q: We developed OLMoTrace to enable researchers, developers, and the general public to inspect where and how language models may have learned to generate certain word sequences.

models.q: OLMoTrace is available today with our three flagship models: OLMo 2 32B Instruct , OLMo 2 13B Instruct , and OLMoE 1B 7B Instruct , and it can be applied to any language model for which you have access to the training data.

unit.q: The highlights indicate long and unique spans that appear verbatim at least once in the training data of this model.

partial_cover.q: Sometimes, a highlighted span may not be present contiguously in any single document, but different parts of that span are present (possibly in different documents) and together they cover the entire span.

limit_nuanced.q: The interpretation of text matches with training data is quite nuanced.

name_verify.q: If you personally verify that these documents come from trusted sources, you can gain confidence that this piece of information generated by the model is factually correct.

low_relevance.q: We use a less saturated color to highlight spans with less relevant documents, and they are labeled in the document list as “low relevance.”

creative.q: In creative writing tasks there is less of a need for fact checking, but you can still trace certain LM-generated expressions back to the training documents.

memorization.q: OLMoTrace reveals that this entire expression appears multiple times in the training data, so the model could have easily learned it through memorization.

cutoff_case.q: now we can see that the model may have learned to say August 2023 from the post-training examples listed on the right.

period.q: since its pre-training data has a cutoff of December 2022

limit_early.q: We are still in an early stage in exploring the full potential of this tool

criteria.q: Maximality : The span is not a subspan of another span that meets the above two criteria.

method_index.q: To speed up computation, we index the training data with infini-gram and develop a novel parallel algorithm, reducing the time complexity of span finding from the naive O(L^2 * N) to O(L * log N)

method_k.q: keeps the K spans with the smallest unigram probability, where K = 0.05 * the number of tokens in the model output.

snippets.q: For each kept span, OLMoTrace retrieves up to 10 document snippets enclosing this span from the training data, which are displayed in the side panel. If there are more than 10 documents for a span, a random set of 10 is sampled.

bm25.q: in the document panel we rank all documents by a BM25 score in descending order.

count.q: In total, these five datasets contain about 3.2 billion documents and 4.6 trillion tokens, and OLMoTrace matches against all of them.

code.q: We also release our source code .

paper_abstract.q: OLMoTrace finds and shows verbatim matches between segments of language model output and documents in the training text corpora.

speed.q: our system returns tracing results within a few seconds.

creativity.q: We showcase how it can be used to explore fact checking, hallucination, and the creativity of language models.

license.q: OLMoTrace is publicly available and fully open-source.

authors.q: by Jiacheng Liu and 30 other authors

data-portraits.name: Data Portraits
aka: Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data
data-portraits.operator: the paper's two authors, Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme; the saved source names no institution, and the live interface's operator is unread
data-portraits.kind: artifacts that record training data and allow downstream inspection, proposed for widespread adoption and implemented with data sketching, in a research paper (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks)
data-portraits.record_object: the contents of training datasets, recorded so that a query can answer whether a model has already encountered a given example during training; implemented for The Pile and The Stack

record.in_layer: a portrait records a training dataset; the paper documents a popular language modeling corpus (The Pile) and a code modeling dataset (The Stack)
record.name: not recorded; the saved abstract does not say whether a portrait keeps any author, title or source metadata for a recorded example
record.readback: a membership query against the recorded dataset: the paper poses 'has the model already encountered a given example during training?' and stresses 'fast and space efficient querying'; a live interface is released (unread)
record.makes: not recorded as a product of the model; the paper states the tool 'enables answering questions about test set leakage and model plagiarism', which checks material against the recorded training data

lifecycle.detail: a published paper: v1 6 March 2023, v2 14 December 2023 (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks); whether the live interface is still served is unread

data-portraits.tll_reading: A readback instrument held on the corpus side: a portrait records the dataset so that a work can be tested for membership, which settles #186's 'is the work in the layer' for a recorded corpus. Dataset membership is not proof that a particular model used a passage, and the name and what a model made from the work (#1543's question) are outside what the saved abstract records.

title.q: Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data

authors.q: Authors: Marc Marone , Benjamin Van Durme

opacity.q: Foundation models are trained on increasingly immense and opaque datasets.

question.q: it can be difficult to answer the straightforward question: has the model already encountered a given example during training?

self_description.q: We therefore propose a widespread adoption of Data Portraits: artifacts that record training data and allow for downstream inspection.

properties.q: First we outline the properties of such an artifact and discuss how existing solutions can be used to increase transparency.

method.q: We then propose and implement a solution based on data sketching, stressing fast and space efficient querying.

datasets.q: Using our tools, we document a popular language modeling corpus (The Pile) and a recently released code modeling dataset (The Stack).

answers.q: We show that our solution enables answering questions about test set leakage and model plagiarism.

overhead.q: Our tool is lightweight and fast, costing only 3% of the dataset size in overhead.

interface.q: We release a live interface of our tools at this https URL and call on dataset and model creators to release Data Portraits as a complement to current documentation practices.

literary-ai.name: The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence
literary-ai.operator: a collaboration between the Columbia English Department, the Columbia University Rare Books & Manuscript Library and Columbia University's Digital Scholarship department; the site is copyright Columbia University Libraries
literary-ai.kind: a Columbia RBML exhibit, online in eight cases, on the long shared history of literature and computation through the Columbia Library's holdings
literary-ai.record_object: texts, professional manuals, devices and techniques that promised to make writing easier or to automate it, and algorithmic analyses of literature, on a timeline from circa 1890 to 1970, from plot generators (Wycliffe Hill's Plot Genie, William Wallace Cook's Plotto) to Christopher Strachey's love letter program and Margaret Masterman's machine translation work

record.in_layer: not applicable: the exhibition holds library items of circa 1890–1970 and records no text entering a machine-learning model; its about page draws a line from these materials to contemporary machine learning-based tools
record.name: the exhibit names the authors and inventors of its items (Wycliffe Hill, William Wallace Cook, Arthur Blanchard, Henrietta Rose Montague, Christopher Strachey, Margaret Masterman, Harriot Fansler, Georges Polti); how it attributes the machine-written prose and poetry it shows is not recorded on the saved page
record.readback: the items are shown in an online exhibit of eight cases, built with Minicomp/Wax, with a GitHub link; the cases themselves are unread
record.makes: in the exhibit's terms, 'algorithmic composition, such as prose and poetry written by machines', plots produced by plot generators with 'spinning devices or automatic number generators', and analyses that sort narrative into types; it records these as production and analysis

lifecycle.detail: an online exhibit, copyright 2022; whether a physical exhibit ran, and when, is not recorded on the saved page

literary-ai.founded: not stated; the site's copyright line is 2022
literary-ai.tll_reading: A historical field resource for #186's procedural lineage, the delegation of composition to devices and systems, where the machine is method and, in Strachey's program, writer. Its timeline closes about 1970 and it records no text entering a model; the machine reader of #186's fourth column is outside what it holds.

operator.q: The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence is a collaboration between the Columbia English Department, the Columbia University Rare Books & Manuscript Library, and Columbia University’s Digital Scholarship department.

self_description.q: This exhibition explores the long, shared history of literature and computation through the Columbia Library’s holdings.

period.q: Following a timeline from circa 1890–1970, this exhibition explores professional manuals, devices, and techniques that promised to make writing easier—and even to automate it.

makes.q: showcases examples of algorithmic composition, such as prose and poetry written by machines, alongside literature written with the aid of algorithmic and combinatorial devices.

two_stories.q: This exhibition broadly tracks two broad stories related to the literary history of AI: production and analysis.

plot_generators.q: such as Wycliffe Hill’s Plot Genies, and plot generators such as William Wallace Cook’s Plotto series.

patents.q: Automated text generation catalyzed a wave of early 20th-century patents, from Arthur Blanchard’s “movie-writer” machine and Henrietta Rose Montague’s “name selector.”

devices.q: Some how-to manuals incorporated simple plot generators, with spinning devices or automatic number generators that would guide would-be novelists past writers’ block.

strachey.q: from Christopher Strachey, who wrote a love letter program in the 1940s, to Margaret Masterman, a linguist who pioneered the use of computers to aid automatic translation.

influence.q: influence and shape contemporary, machine learning-based tools used in automating aviation accident reports and defense logistics.

analysis.q: The second story tracks the use of algorithms to analyze literature

polti.q: Georges Polti’s Les trente-six situations dramatiques (1895)

storage.q: Information storage was increasingly understood to be central both to analysis and to composition.

license.q: © Copyright 2022, Columbia University Libraries. Contents offered with a CC-BY 4.0 International License

common-crawl.name: Common Crawl
common-crawl.operator: the Common Crawl Foundation, a 501(c)(3) non-profit founded in 2007; Wikipedia names Gil Elbaz as founder and Rich Skrenta as executive director
common-crawl.kind: free, open repository of web crawl data
common-crawl.record_object: pages of the open web, crawled each month: over 300 billion pages spanning 15 years, with 3 to 5 billion new pages added each month

record.in_layer: whatever its crawler captured from the open web; Wikipedia reports that AI companies began training large language models on the data in the 2020s, that ChatGPT as of 2023 was largely trained on it, and that refined datasets (FineWeb, DCLM, C4) are built from its raw data
record.name: not recorded: the saved sources state no author or attribution field; a page is held by URL, with its metadata extracts and text extracts
record.readback: a page can be searched by URL in the Common Crawl URL Index (also a CDXJ Index); the corpus can be downloaded whole or in part. Wikipedia reports The Atlantic's November 2025 finding that the public search function showed no entries for sites that had requested removal while those sites were still in the scrapes
record.makes: not recorded on its own pages; per Wikipedia, other organizations refine its raw data into datasets (FineWeb, DCLM, C4), and AI companies train large language models on the data

lifecycle.detail: monthly crawls; latest listed CC-MAIN-2026-43; October 2026 web graph announced on the home page

common-crawl.tll_reading: The archive reads Common Crawl as the receiving apparatus's first intake, the plainest case of #186's persistence criterion: the place 'where the training and retrieval layers actually look', entered by being on the open web and addressed by URL. What is made from a page (refined datasets, trained models) is made downstream by others, as Wikipedia reports; crawl inclusion can be inspected in the URL Index, use of a captured page in a given model's training is a further claim its own pages do not make, and Wikipedia's report of The Atlantic's finding marks the limit of the index as a witness. A work's name survives there only as far as it is written into the page itself.

self_description.q: Common Crawl maintains a free, open repository of web crawl data that can be used by anyone.

operator.q: Common Crawl is a 501(c)(3) non–profit founded in 2007.

purpose.q: We make wholesale extraction, transformation, and analysis of open web data accessible to researchers.

cadence.q: 3–5 billion new pages added each month.

web_graph.q: We are extremely pleased to announce the release of our October 2026 Web Graph, comprising data from August, September, and October 2026.

petabytes.q: The Common Crawl corpus contains petabytes of data, regularly collected since 2008.

unit.q: The corpus contains raw web page data, metadata extracts, and text extracts.

storage.q: Common Crawl data is stored on Amazon Web Services’ Public Data Sets and on multiple academic cloud platforms across the world.

access.q: Access to the corpus hosted by Amazon is free.

download.q: You may use Amazon’s cloud platform to run analysis jobs directly against it or you can download it, whole or in part.

readback.q: You can search for pages in our corpus using the Common Crawl URL Index.

indexes.q: Overview CDXJ Index URL Index Web Graphs Latest Crawl Crawl Stats Graph Stats Errata

founder.q: Common Crawl was founded by Gil Elbaz .

director.q: Rich Skrenta is the executive director.

costs_wp.q: Access to the data is free on Amazon Web Services , but users may incur storage and compute costs.

publishing_2011.q: It began publishing its crawls in 2011.

blekko.q: which started by crawling a list of URLs donated by the search engine Blekko .

in_layer_llm.q: The data had mostly been primarily used by researchers and some startups until the 2020s, when AI companies started training large language models using the data.

in_layer_chatgpt.q: ChatGPT , as of 2023, was largely trained on Common Crawl,

pile_wp.q: By 2024, The Pile and Common Crawl had been the two main training datasets being used to train AI models.

atlantic.q: It included misleading results in the public search function on its website that showed no entries for websites that had requested their archives be removed, when in fact those sites were still included in its scrapes used by AI companies.

atlantic_date.q: In November 2025, an investigation by technology journalist Alex Reisner for The Atlantic revealed that Common Crawl misled publishers when it claimed it respected paywalls in its scraping

ai_funding.q: In 2023, it began receiving significant financial support from AI companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI , each of which donated $250,000.

ccbot_blocked.q: As of 2025, Reisner found that CCBot was the most widely-blocked bot by the top 1000 websites.

refined.q: A number of organizations take raw Common Crawl data and refine it into datasets that exclude edgy content or are otherwise higher-quality for their purposes, such as FineWeb, DCLM and C4.

wayback_wp.q: Common Crawl was designed to have more and fresher data that was more efficient to analyze and utilize than the Wayback Machine created by the Internet Archive .

hugging_face_wp.q: In April 2026, Common Crawl experimentally began to distribute its data through Hugging Face Storage Bucket , in addition to its standard storage on Amazon S3 .

project-gutenberg.name: Project Gutenberg
project-gutenberg.operator: the Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation, which operates Project Gutenberg and accepts donations; per Wikipedia, a 501(c)(3) chartered in Mississippi in 2000, with Eric Hellman acting CEO after Gregory Newby died in 2025
project-gutenberg.record_object: 'the world's literature' digitized and proofread by volunteers; per Wikipedia, mostly full texts of books or individual stories in the public domain in the United States, primarily works of literature from the Western cultural tradition, most in English

record.in_layer: public domain eBooks; per Wikipedia, the Pile carries a 'Gutenberg (PG-19)' component of 11.68 GB; Project Gutenberg's own saved pages say nothing of training
record.name: not recorded for authors in the saved own pages; Wikipedia records that 'Project Gutenberg' is a trademark that cannot be used in commercial or modified redistributions, that public domain texts may be resold once all references to Project Gutenberg are removed, and that books have been sold stripped of attribution to the project
record.readback: each eBook has a permanent landing page; site search; a Gutenberg index file listing all books and a machine-readable catalog database (Offline Catalogs and Feeds); the website itself 'is intended for human users only', and bulk downloads go through mirrors
record.makes: not recorded on its own pages; downstream, per Wikipedia, the Pile carries a 'Gutenberg (PG-19)' component, and NaNoGenMo's rules allow a generated 'novel' that grabs 'a random novel from Project Gutenberg'

lifecycle.detail: operating since 1971; per Wikipedia, about 30 new eBooks a week (May 2025)

project-gutenberg.tll_reading: The archive reads Project Gutenberg as a source library held apart from the datasets made from it. Its own terms address two readers: the website 'is intended for human users only', and bulk and machine access go to mirrors and a machine-readable catalog. Its texts reach training and composition downstream, in the Pile's Gutenberg (PG-19) component (Wikipedia) and as allowed raw material for NaNoGenMo's generated novels; the name a text carries after that passage is outside its own pages, and Wikipedia records texts resold with references to the project removed.

founder.q: Michael Hart, founder of Project Gutenberg, invented eBooks in 1971

method.q: Since then, thousands of volunteers have digitized and diligently proofread the world’s literature.

free.q: All Project Gutenberg eBooks are completely free and always will be.

mission.q: To encourage the creation and distribution of eBooks.

operator.q: The Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation , which operates Project Gutenberg and accepts donations.

audience.q: Project Gutenberg’s target audience is United States persons over 13 years of age.

hathitrust.tll_reading: The archive reads HathiTrust in three layers kept apart: holdings (volumes digitized via Google Books, the Internet Archive and the libraries), access (restricted where copyright status cannot be established), and computational availability (the Research Center's, now ended). Authors Guild v. HathiTrust, as Wikipedia reports it, is the record's precedent for a machine reading of whole books whose product is a finding (search) while the pages stay closed; the saved sources tie none of its volumes to model training.

the-pile.tll_reading: The archive reads the Pile as the training layer named and itemized: a work enters by belonging to a component (Books3, PG-19, Pile-CC), and what the receiving apparatus makes from it is a trained model, scored on the Pile's own benchmark. Its own pages offer no per-work search; the corpus has since been inspected from outside (Data Portraits documents it), and Wikipedia's record of the Books3 removal and the authors' suit is the field's clearest case of works found in the layer under their authors' names after the fact.

What a model makes from a given work, and whether the work is carried with 'the metadata that lets it be found and attributed' (#186), are outside the saved abstract; the dataset card that would show document fields was rate-limited.

cell.tll_reading: The archive reads CELL as the field's meta-aggregator, a discovery layer over member archives (ELMCIP among them, itself frozen since October 2026): its metadata is published as linked data (SPARQL, Wikidata) under each work's author, the machine-legible, attributed form in which a work can be found, and it states its aim as keeping works 'discoverable and preserved across generations of computational technology'. Its indexed records still need work-level relevance judgments before any of them bears on this census's question.

nanogenmo.name: NaNoGenMo
nanogenmo.operator: its official admins @dariusk and @hugovk; the community is organised in GitHub repositories, one per edition; based on an idea Darius Kazemi tweeted
nanogenmo.kind: an annual month-long activity: write code that generates a novel of 50k+ words, organised as a community on GitHub
nanogenmo.record_object: code-generated novels of 50,000 words or more and their source code, shared by participants each November since 2013

record.in_layer: not recorded; the rules allow a 'novel' made from existing text (it 'could literally grab a random novel from Project Gutenberg') and point to corpora, a repository of public domain lists
record.name: a participant declares intent in an issue under their own GitHub account; the saved page states no rule on how a generated novel is credited, and the source code 'does not have to be licensed in a particular way'
record.readback: each edition's repository issues, with a resources issue per edition, 2013 to 2025
record.makes: a generated 'novel' of 50k+ words shared with its source code; the rules allow it to be made from existing text ('grab a random novel from Project Gutenberg'), and each edition pools libraries, corpuses, APIs and techniques in a resources issue

lifecycle.detail: editions every November from 2013 to 2025 listed; the saved page, read on 1 November 2026, lists no 2026 edition

nanogenmo.tll_reading: The archive reads NaNoGenMo as an inspectable program/output community in the machine-composition direction: each novel is shared with its code under a participant's account, so what a program makes from its source texts (a Project Gutenberg novel, a pooled corpus) can be read beside the program that made it. Practice varies by participant: crediting of the generated text and of any source it draws on is left to each ('ultimately it's on your head'), so a claim about an edition rests on its particular repositories.

self_description.q: National Novel Generation Month - based on an idea Darius Kazemi tweeted on a whim .

goal.q: Spend the month of November writing code that generates a novel of 50k+ words. This is in the spirit of National Novel Writing Month 's interesting definition of a novel as 50,000 words of fiction.

rule.q: The only rule is that you share at least one novel and also your source code at the end.

code_license.q: The source code does not have to be licensed in a particular way, so long as you share it. The code itself does not need to be on GitHub, either.

github.q: We're just using this repo as a place to organize the community.

novel_defined.q: The "novel" is defined however you want. It could be 50,000 repetitions of the word "meow". It could literally grab a random novel from Project Gutenberg.

copyright.q: Please try to respect copyright. We're not going to police it, as ultimately it's on your head if you want to just copy/paste a Stephen King novel or whatever

period.q: This activity starts at 12:01am GMT on Nov 1st and ends at 12:01am GMT Dec 1st.

participate.q: Open an issue on the edition's repo and declare your intent to participate.

diaries.q: Feel free to post dev diaries, sample output, etc.

admins.q: Official admins for NaNoGenMo are @dariusk and @hugovk.

resources.q: There's an open issue for each edition where you can add resources (libraries, corpuses, APIs, techniques, etc).

corpora.q: You might want to check out corpora , a repository of public domain lists of things
